question: Who washed Jesus's feet with her tears and dried his feet with her hair?
summary: John 12:1-3 names Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, anointing Jesus' feet at Bethany six days before Passover. Luke 7:36-38 places an unnamed sinful woman washing Jesus' feet with her tears at a Pharisee's house earlier in the ministry. Both narratives describe the same striking detail — a woman wiping Jesus' feet with her hair — but identify different women in different settings, and a long interpretive tradition further conflated both with Mary Magdalene.

reconcile.connective: JFB flatly denies any textual ground for identifying Luke's unnamed sinner with a named woman, keeping her distinct from John's Mary of Bethany.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss noted Luke and John describe the distinctive foot-drying-with-hair detail 'in nearly the same words,' concluding this is one story, not two.

skeptic.name: David Friedrich Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined
skeptic.attribution: David Friedrich Strauss (1808-1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (German orig. Das Leben Jesu, 1835-36; Eng. trans. 1846), Part II, § 89.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley lists this exact pairing under events distinguished by occurring at different times: "Christ anointed at one time, Matt. xxvi. 7; John xii. 3; at another time, Luke vii. 37, 38 (the best critics hold that the anointing in the first two passages was quite distinct from that mentioned by Luke)," p. 411.

excerpts.source_note_text:
CHRIST'S FEET WASHED WITH TEARS. (Luk 7:36-50)
a sinner--one who had led a profligate life. Note.--There is no ground whatever for the popular notion that this woman was Mary Magdalene, nor do we know what her name was. (See on Luk 8:2.)
an alabaster box of ointment--a perfume vessel, in some cases very costly (Joh 12:5). "The ointment has here a peculiar interest, as the offering by a penitent of what had been an accessory in her unhallowed work of sin" [ALFORD].
